catalog_quote: Die Akzente im Kiṅamwezi. Der Haupt-, ebenso wie der Nebenakzent kann auf jeder Silbe gefunden werden: 1. Der Hauptakzent oder Hauptton ... a) auf der Ultima ... b) auf der Penultima ... c) auf der Antepenultima ... d) auf der Prae-Antepenultima ... e) auf der Ante-Prae-Antepenultima ... 2. Der Nebenakzent oder Nebenton ... a) auf der Ultima ... b) auf der Penultima ... c) auf der Antepenultima ... d) auf der Prae-Antepenultima ... e) auf der Ante-Prae-Antepenultima ... Wie zu jedem Berg ein Tal gehört, so ist das Auftreten des Haupttones ohne Nebenton undenkbar. Absolut einsilbige Wörter sind deshalb jedes Akzentes bar. Die häufigste Form des Auftretens ist die, daß bei zweisilbigen Wörtern (bzw. dreisilbigen, aber zweisilbigen Stämmen) Penultima den Hauptakzent Ultima den Nebenakzent bekommt, also ... bzw. .... Dementsprechend erhält bei nur einsilbigen Stimmen [sic, print; = Stämmen] das Verbal- oder Nominalpräfix den Hauptakzent, der eigentliche Stamm dagegen nur den Nebenakzent, vorausgesetzt, daß er ohne angehängtes Suffix, Enklitik usw. tatsächlich die Ultima bildet. [p. 122] Außer der soeben genannten sind folgende Kombinationen von Haupt- und Nebenakzent die gebräuchlichsten ... [p. 125] Selbstverständlich gibt es auch noch andere Kombinationsmöglichkeiten ... [p. 126] Noch einige Beispiele, in denen Haupt- oder Nebenakzent auf der fünftletzten Silbe (also 1e oder 2e) und der Hauptakzent auf der sechstletzten Silbe vorkommt
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Nyamwezi (nyam1276) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title listed one title, Dahl 1904 'Die Töne und Akzente im KiNamwezi' (MSOS 7, Abt. III: 106-126, Glottolog 132479); the whole MSOS vol. 7 was already held by the project from archive.org (item mitteilungen07berluoft) and I re-read the accent section and verified it on the p.121 page scan. Dahl separates pitch tone (pp. 106-120) from dynamic accent (pp. 121-126) and states that main and secondary accent can fall on any syllable, that the most frequent pattern is penultimate main accent + final secondary accent (prefix takes the main accent with monosyllabic stems), and lists further combinations with main accent as far left as the sixth-from-last syllable. This is the best first-hand stress statement for the language read in this search of works with stress in the title; there is no catalog's classification to confirm or contradict. Nothing remained unread among the works with stress in the title (priority none). the on-disk already lists unopened later works (Nurse & Maganga 1979; Maganga & Schadeberg 1992 body; Schadeberg 1989/2005; Steere 1882) whose stress content is unknown. new_statements.quote: Der Haupt-, ebenso wie der Nebenakzent kann auf jeder Silbe gefunden werden: [...] Wie zu jedem Berg ein Tal gehört, so ist das Auftreten des Haupttones ohne Nebenton undenkbar. Absolut einsilbige Wörter sind deshalb jedes Akzentes bar. Die häufigste Form des Auftretens ist die, daß bei zweisilbigen Wörtern (bzw. dreisilbigen, aber zweisilbigen Stämmen) Penultima den Hauptakzent, Ultima den Nebenakzent bekommt [...]. Dementsprechend erhält bei nur einsilbigen Stämmen das Verbal- oder Nominalpräfix den Hauptakzent, der eigentliche Stamm dagegen nur den Nebenakzent, vorausgesetzt, daß er ohne angehängtes Suffix, Enklitik usw. tatsächlich die Ultima bildet.
new_statements.translation: The main accent, like the secondary accent, can be found on any syllable: [...] As every mountain has its valley, so the occurrence of the main accent without a secondary accent is unthinkable. Strictly monosyllabic words therefore have no accent at all. The most frequent pattern is that in disyllabic words (or trisyllabic words with disyllabic stems) the penult receives the main accent and the ultima the secondary accent [...]. Accordingly, with monosyllabic stems the verbal or nominal prefix receives the main accent and the stem itself only the secondary accent, provided that, without an added suffix, enclitic etc., it actually forms the ultima.
new_statements.citation: Dahl, E[dmund]. 1904. Die Töne und Akzente im Kinamwezi. Mitteilungen des Seminars für Orientalische Sprachen zu Berlin 7, Abt. III (Afrikanische Studien): 106-126.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Checked the page scan we hold (running head 'Dahl: Die Töne und Akzente im Kiṅamwezi. 121') and the scanned slice lines 1259-1301. The section heading 'Die Akzente im Kiṅamwezi' and every quoted sentence are on p.121 as quoted; the only differences are (a) the report's '[..]' elides the schema list 1a-e/2a-e and the phrase 'bekommt, also ˘́˘̀ bzw. ˘˘́˘̀', and (b) the print reads 'bei nur einsilbigen Stimmen' (a printer's error) where the quote silently normalizes to 'Stämmen'. Reading: I agree with tone language with a stress statement. Dahl's article is in two parts: pp.106-120 'Die eigentlichen Töne im Kinamwezi' state where the Hochton and Tiefton fall (contracted genitive regens ultima,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dahl (a Moravian missionary at Urambo) separates pitch tones ('eigentliche Töne', with a Hochton whose positions he lists) from dynamic accents. He says main and secondary accent can occur on any syllable, but the default is main accent on the penultimate and secondary on the final syllable (so the prefix carries the main accent when the stem is monosyllabic); pp.122-126 then list six other main/secondary combinations, including accent on the 4th-, 5th- and 6th-last syllables in long derived verbs and reduplications. His accented examples (e.g. ku-fwilá, vafwá, ku-göngola) look like the H-tone / high-tone-shift patterns that Schadeberg (1991) and Kanijo (2019) describe, so the 'accent' is probably not independent of tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicit: every polysyllabic word has both a Hauptakzent and a Nebenakzent; default Nebenakzent on the ultima when the main accent is penultimate; other placements listed in groups I-VI.
new_statements.exceptions: Any syllable may bear either accent; groups II-VI list antepenultimate and earlier main accents (long extended verbs, full reduplications, e.g. ku-gelekelezya, ku-yanukulizya). Meinhof 1904 (same volume, p.241), working from four speakers, contradicts Dahl: the lengthening ('mechanical') accent 'seems to prefer the antepenult and to stay on the initial syllable even in four-syllable words', but 'the rule is not clear to me'. Modern descriptions (Schadeberg 1991; Kanijo 2019; Maganga & Schadeberg 1992 per its TOC) describe Nyamwezi purely as a two-tone language with high tone shift and say nothing about stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms and short phrases, Urambo/Kigalaganza dialect area (with Sisumbwa comparisons); Meinhof's remarks are from elicited isolated words. Confidence low: 1904 missionary description whose 'accent' marks likely conflate H tone; no modern source states a stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Dahl 1904 describes the Nyamwezi of Urambo (Kigalaganza dialect, with Sisumbwa comparisons); Meinhof 1904 elicited from four Nyamwezi speakers in Germany/East Africa; Velten 1901 is the Unyanyembe dialect; Maganga & Schadeberg 1992 and Kanijo 2019 describe the Ndala (Nzega District) variety. All are Nyamwezi proper (nyam1276); no separate glottocode assigned here for the Galaganza dialect.

new_statements.quote: Was die Betonung der Wörter betrifft, so ist dieselbe bei dem schnellen Sprechen der Leute sehr schwer erkennbar. Spricht er schnell, so betont er meist die Endsilben, doch legt er stets den Nachdruck auf den Stamm des Wortes; oft wird aber durch das Näseln und Dehnen der Wörter die Betonung verwischt. Sehr beeinträchtigt wird die Klarstellung der Betonung durch Ausstoßung von Vokalen [...]. Die Betonung fällt dann zumeist auf die Stelle, an der ein Vokal ausgefallen ist. [...] Es ist mir darum nicht möglich, feste Gesetze darin aufzustellen. Hervorzuheben wäre eventuell hier: kutŭ́la schlagen und kutū́la setzen, stellen; kulā́la schlafen und kulála fliegen; kutúngula losbinden und kutungū́la strafen mit Schlägen u. a.
new_statements.translation: As for the stress of words, it is very hard to make out in the people's fast speech. When he speaks fast he mostly stresses the final syllables, yet he always puts the emphasis on the stem of the word; but often the stress is blurred by nasalizing and drawing out the words. Establishing the stress is much impaired by the elision of vowels [...]. The stress then mostly falls on the place where a vowel has dropped out. [...] It is therefore not possible for me to set up fixed laws here. Worth pointing out perhaps: kutŭ́la 'beat' and kutū́la 'set, place'; kulā́la 'sleep' and kulála 'fly'; kutúngula 'untie' and kutungū́la 'punish with blows', etc.
new_statements.citation: Stern, R[udolf]. 1906. Eine Kinyamwezigrammatik. Mitteilungen des Seminars für Orientalische Sprachen zu Berlin IX, Abt. III (Afrikanische Studien): 129-258.

Spricht er schnell, so betont er meist die Endsilben, doch legt er stets den Nachdruck auf den Stamm des Wortes; oft wird aber durch das Naeseln und Dehnen der Woerter die Betonung verwischt. Sehr beeintraechtigt wird die Klarstellung der Betonung…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The author cannot state a fixed stress position: prominence is on the verb/noun stem, in fast speech final syllables sound stressed, elision sites attract stress, and he gives accent/length-marked minimal pairs (kutŭ́la vs kutū́la etc.) showing that prominence placement/vowel length distinguishes words; explicitly 'no fixed laws'. No tonal analysis (pre-tonological description of what is now known to be a tone language cluster).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shifts to the site of an elided vowel (word-final elision, compounding: nzila mbi 'bad road' vs nzilámbi 'danger'); lexical pairs distinguished only by accent/length marks.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level remarks drawn from connected fast speech and school dictation; author notes speakers contract words and drop particles, so citation-form vs phrase stress is not separated. Section A adds a three-way vowel-length description (over-long vowel followed by a very short syllable).
new_statements.identity_note: Stern (Moravian missionary at Kitunda/Kiwere, south of Tabora) titles the work 'Kinyamwezi' and says explicitly it is not dialectally pure: it reflects the speech along the Ubagwe-Kiwere line, incl. the Vakonongo, i.e. the southern Nyamwezi lingua franca the people call 'Kilugaluga'. Glottolog files it under Konongo-Ruwila (kono1265) on the authority of Whiteley & Gutkind 1958 ('Deals with the Konongo dialect'). Nothing found for the Ruwila (rwl) half of the languoid. Masele 2001's tonal remark is a Zone-F-wide generalization, not Konongo-specific. Note the Glottolog record's year/volume (1905, VIII) should read 1906, Jahrgang IX, Abt. III.

new_statements.quote: Absolut einsilbige Wörter sind deshalb jedes Akzentes bar. Die häufigste Form des Auftretens ist die, daß bei zweisilbigen Wörtern (bzw. dreisilbigen, aber zweisilbigen Stämmen) Penultima den Hauptakzent, Ultima den Nebenakzent bekommt, also ˊˋ bzw. _ˊˋ. Dementsprechend erhält bei nur einsilbigen Stämmen das Verbal- oder Nominalpräfix den Hauptakzent, der eigentliche Stamm dagegen nur den Nebenakzent, vorausgesetzt, daß er ohne angehängtes Suffix, Enklitik usw. tatsächlich die Ultima bildet.
new_statements.translation: Absolutely monosyllabic words are therefore devoid of any accent. The most frequent pattern is that in disyllabic words (or trisyllabic words with disyllabic stems) the penult receives the main accent and the ultima the secondary accent, i.e. ˊˋ or _ˊˋ. Correspondingly, with monosyllabic stems the verbal or nominal prefix receives the main accent and the stem itself only the secondary accent, provided that, without an attached suffix, enclitic etc., it really forms the ultima.
new_statements.citation: Dahl, Edmund. 1904. Die Töne und Akzente im KiNamwezi. Mitteilungen des Seminars für Orientalische Sprachen zu Berlin 7, Abt. III (Afrikanische Studien): 106-126.
new_statements.reading: First-hand missionary description (Urambo dialect area, 1904): a dynamic main accent distinct from pitch tone; the commonest placement is penultimate main accent + final secondary accent, but Dahl states at the outset that both accents 'can be found on any syllable' and documents (pp. 122-126) main accent on the antepenult and further left, up to the sixth-from-last syllable, especially in reduplicated and long derived verb stems. So: penultimate-default with lexically variable placement, not a fixed penultimate rule. Meinhof 1904 (same volume, p. 241, also held by the project) independently reports a 'mechanische Ton' that in Namwezi 'seems to like to stand on the third-from-last syllable' but admits the rule was unclear to him; later tone-based work (Schadeberg 1991; Maganga & Schadeberg 1992 TOC; Kanijo 2019) makes no stress statement.

tone_statements.citation: Joilet, Kamil. 2015. Common characteristics in Sukuma-Nyamwezi transitional dialects. MA (Linguistics) dissertation, The University of Dodoma. hdl:20.500.12661/732.
tone_statements.quote: The results from the findings show that there are differences in stress between Ndala and Iskisya dialects because in Isikisya the first syllable is always stressed ... In Ndala the first and last syllables are always stressed ... both have fixed stress ... Thus, pitch variation in Ndala and Isikisya does not distinguish words, either lexically or grammatically. ... Syllables are V or CV and have four tones on short vowels: high, low, rising, and falling (Rahma, 2006).
tone_statements.locator: ch. 4, pp. 43-44 (subsections 'Stress', 'Intonation') and the 'Syllable' paragraph before section 4.6
tone_statements.summary: Author asserts fixed word stress (initial in Isikisya; initial+final in Ndala) and non-distinctive pitch, yet also cites a four-way tone contrast (H, L, rising, falling) on short vowels from a secondary source; no analysis or tone-marked data.

tone_statements.citation: Yukawa, Yasutoshi (湯川恭敏). 2002. ニャムウェズィ語アクセント試論 [A Tentative Tonal Analysis of Nyamwezi Verbs]. アジア・アフリカ文法研究 / Asian and African Linguistics (AALL) 31: 45-118. Tokyo: Research Institute for Languages and Cultures of Asia and Africa (ILCAA), Tokyo University of Foreign Studies. ISBN 4-87297-834-X. (Repository issue date 2002-03-31; CiNii/KAKEN product record gives 2003.)
tone_statements.quote: アクセントは、母音字および子音前鼻音字上の ´ で「高」を、＾で下降調を、ˇ で上昇調を、無印で「低」をあらわす。下降調と上昇調は末尾にのみあらわれるが、後者は直前が高いと発音上は消滅し低くなるようである。また、直前が低い場合、上昇調は「高」と区別しにくいだけでなく、「低」と区別しにくい場合も多い。 ... この言語の動詞自体は元来のアクセントの型 ... の対立を保存している。
tone_statements.translation: Accent [tone] is written with ´ over a vowel letter or a pre-consonantal nasal letter for 'High', ^ for a falling tone, ˇ for a rising tone, and no mark for 'Low'. Falling and rising tones occur only word-finally, and the latter apparently disappears in pronunciation and becomes low when the preceding [syllable] is high. Moreover, when the preceding [syllable] is low, the rising tone is not only hard to distinguish from 'High' but often also hard to distinguish from 'Low'. ... The verbs of this language themselves preserve the original opposition of accent [tone] types [called Type A and Type B].
tone_statements.locator: p. 45 (はじめに / introduction) and p. 46; informant and survey details p. 116 note 1; conclusion 'おわりに' p. 115
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Surface tones on vowels and pre-consonantal (moraic) nasals: High vs unmarked Low, plus Falling and Rising confined to word-final position; final Rising is neutralised (realised low) after a High and is often hard to hear after a Low, but is diagnosable because a word-final High/Rising raises the initial syllables of a following noun (tone sandhi); verbs keep the inherited two-class lexical tone…

tone_statements.citation: Schadeberg, Thilo C. 1989. Tone and history of Nyamwezi verb forms with complex final tones. Afrika und Übersee 72: 33-42.
tone_statements.quote: The first of these I call "High Tone Shift" (HTS). It says that any high tone is realized not on the mora to which it inherently belongs, but on the following mora. (Certain complications arising in the context of long and double vowels are omitted in this statement.) [...] In this paradigm only the root, that is the first mora of the verb stem, is tonally distinctive; a high tone of a root is realized on the second mora of the stem. [...] EA: In verb forms, all tone bearing positions between the root and the Final have the same tone as (the first tone bearing element of) that Final.
tone_statements.locator: printed pp. 33-34; section 1 'The Tone of the Past and the Perfect in Nyamwezi'
tone_statements.check: quotation from the author's open copy, read 2026-09-25; not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: Catalog has classification tonal with an empty rule; the work states the two general tone rules of the language: (1) High Tone Shift, every H surfaces one mora to the right of its underlying mora (tone-bearing unit = mora; long and double vowels bring unstated complications); (2) Extension Assimilation, a structure condition on verb forms: extensions take the tone of the Final. sources.quote: The Nyamwezi speak in rather a drawling, snuffling manner, raising the voice slightly on the final vowel of their words, and making no very marked accent on any other syllable.
sources.note: Steere's handbooks typically open with a note on accent (his Swahili handbook states penultimate accent); would give an independent 19th-century statement for the Unyanyembe dialect.

sources.note: The only prosodic statement in the 34-page grammar: vowels are short except in the word's 'Tonsilbe' (stressed syllable), i.e. the stressed vowel is lengthened. tone.translation: Accent [tone] is written with ´ over a vowel letter or a pre-consonantal nasal letter for 'High', ^ for a falling tone, ˇ for a rising tone, and no mark for 'Low'. Falling and rising tones occur only word-finally, and the latter apparently disappears in pronunciation and becomes low when the preceding [syllable] is high. Moreover, when the preceding [syllable] is low, the rising tone is not only hard to distinguish from 'High' but often also hard to distinguish from 'Low'. ... The verbs of this language themselves preserve the original opposition of accent [tone] types [called Type A and Type B].
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: Surface tones on vowels and pre-consonantal (moraic) nasals: High vs unmarked Low, plus Falling and Rising confined to word-final position; final Rising is neutralised (realised low) after a High and is often hard to hear after a Low, but is diagnosable because a word-final High/Rising raises the initial syllables of a following noun (tone sandhi); verbs keep the inherited two-class lexical tone…

sources.quote: The first of these I call "High Tone Shift" (HTS). It says that any high tone is realized not on the mora to which it inherently belongs, but on the following mora. (Certain complications arising in the context of long and double vowels are omitted in this statement.) [...] In this paradigm only the root, that is the first mora of the verb stem, is tonally distinctive; a high tone of a root is realized on the second mora of the stem. [...] EA: In verb forms, all tone bearing positions between the root and the Final have the same tone as (the first tone bearing element of) that Final.
